articles.title: UK woman whose life was âsavedâ by a cancer trial cycles 186 miles to thank the hospital that gave her hope
articles.summary: UK News: Julie Rose, a 49-year-old woman from Bridgwater, Somerset, has taken on a 186-mile cycle ride to The Royal Marsden in London after a clinical trial ga.
articles.body: Julie Rose, a 49-year-old woman from Bridgwater, Somerset, has taken on a 186-mile cycle ride to The Royal Marsden in London after a clinical trial gave her renewed hope following a devastating cancer diagnosis. Rose was diagnosed with rare medullary thyroid cancer in 2020, after initially putting the back pain she experienced while training for a half-marathon down to wear and tear from an earlier hip replacement. Months later, discovering a lump in her neck led to the diagnosis that changed her life. Her cancer had already spread to her adrenal glands and liver when she was referred to The Royal Marsden. With limited treatment options available, Rose was offered a place on a clinical trial in May 2021. She chose to take the opportunity, and within six months, her tumours had shrunk by 60%. She remains on the medication and says scans continue to bring encouraging results.How cancer diagnosis changed Roseâs lifeRose first noticed something was wrong in March 2020 while training for a half-marathon. Back pain began interfering with her running, but because she had previously undergone a hip replacement, she initially believed the discomfort was simply related to her old injury. The situation became much more serious when she later discovered a lump in her neck. According to Just Giving, doctors diagnosed her with medullary thyroid cancer, a rare form of thyroid cancer that develops in the thyroid's specialised C cells. For Rose, the diagnosis was particularly frightening because she had three children and a partner. She described the moment as one in which her âworld just stoppedâ, as the family faced the uncertainty surrounding an advanced cancer diagnosis. By the time she reached The Royal Marsden, the cancer had spread to her adrenal glands and liver. Her treatment choices were limited, but she was offered an opportunity that could potentially change the course of her illness.The clinical trial that changed her outlookRose became one of a small number of patients in the UK given access to the clinical trial. She said there were only around nine or 10 places available nationally, making the opportunity particularly significant. Faced with the choice between an older drug that she feared would make her feel unwell and the new treatment being investigated through the trial, Rose decided to take what she described as a gamble. She began the new medication in May 2021 and has continued taking it. The results have given her reason to be optimistic. Within six months, her tumours had shrunk by 60%, while subsequent scans have continued to bring good news. Rose said some of her tumours have completely disappeared and that she feels well while taking the drug. Her experience also demonstrates why clinical trials are an important part of cancer research. Trials allow researchers to investigate treatments that may eventually provide additional options for patients whose cancers are difficult to treat.From cancer treatment to a 186-mile fundraising challengeAfter receiving treatment, Rose returned to cycling and decided to turn the activity into a personal tribute to the medical team that helped her. She began her 186-mile journey in Bridgwater and planned to finish at The Royal Marsden in London. The challenge combines something she loves with her desire to support the institution that played such an important role in her treatment. Rose has previously taken part in the London to Paris Cycle, but this ride carries a much more personal meaning. Rather than simply completing another endurance challenge, she is cycling towards the hospital where she received treatment and where research continues into advanced thyroid cancers. She said she wanted to make the journey personal because of the positive results she has continued to receive from her scans. Her fundraising will support The Royal Marsden's work, including research aimed at improving cancer diagnosis and developing more personalised treatments.Why cancer research matters beyond one patientThe Royal Marsden has played a leading role in research into advanced thyroid cancers, with clinical trials exploring new approaches to treatment. Rose's story illustrates the human impact that such research can have when experimental treatments eventually provide patients with new possibilities. For her, the ride is an opportunity to acknowledge the doctors, nurses, researchers and support staff involved in her care while helping fund future work. Antonia Dalmahoy, managing director of The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, told BBC that Rose's fundraising would contribute towards research focused on earlier cancer diagnosis and better, more personalised treatments for patients in the UK and around the world. Rose's journey is therefore about more than the distance covered on a bicycle. It represents the years between a frightening diagnosis and a future she can once again plan for. After being told she had advanced cancer, she now has the chance to cycle towards the hospital that helped give her that future back.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hungarian Gripen fighter jet crashes: Pilot ejects safely, probe launched
articles.summary: Europe News: A Hungarian Air Force Gripen fighter jet crashed near the town of Szolnok on Monday, with the pilot successfully ejecting from the aircraft, prime min.
articles.body: A Hungarian Air Force Gripen fighter jet crashed near the town of Szolnok on Monday, with the pilot successfully ejecting from the aircraft, prime minister Péter Magyar said.The pilot survived and was taken to hospital, while no other injuries or damage to civilian infrastructure were reported.“For reasons that are not yet known, a Gripen fighter jet of the Hungarian Defence Forces crashed a few minutes ago near Szolnok. The pilot successfully ejected. An investigation is under way, and the defence minister is on his way to the scene,” Magyar wrote on Facebook.Hungarian defence minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi later said the pilot had survived and was taken to hospital by ambulance.“The pilot is in an ambulance, he is alive,” Ruszin-Szendi said in a Facebook video.The PM also said, “According to a preliminary report, there were no injuries and there was no harm in civilian infrastructure.”The Hungarian army also has an air base near Szolnok. AP quoted Szolnok mayor Mihály Gyorfi as saying the pilot “was probably training as usual” at the helicopter base outside the city, while confirming that there were no known injuries from the crash.Hungary, a NATO member, operates 18 JAS 39 Gripen fighter aircraft based at Kecskemét. Fourteen were acquired through a lease-purchase programme launched in 2001, while four additional Gripens ordered in 2024 joined the fleet this year.The Hungarian Gripens regularly participate in international operations. In the second half of last year, the aircraft also took part in protecting the airspace of the Baltic states. The cause of Monday’s crash remains unclear.Hungary previously experienced a Gripen accident in 2015, when a fighter crash-landed in central Hungary because of a technical fault. The pilot ejected and the aircraft was later repaired.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US threatens toughest sanctions yet against Iran: What we know
articles.summary: Tehran has threatened to retaliate against any country that joins new US economic measures.
articles.body:
With diplomacy stalled over ending the war on Iran , Washington is seeking to ratchet up pressure on Tehran with “unprecedented” economic pressure.

After United States President Donald Trump threatened to punish any country doing business with Tehran last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that a new series of economic measures will “collapse” the Iranian government, calling on countries to join the effort.

On Saturday, Tehran threatened to retaliate against any country that joins the US in economic sanctions against it.

Here’s what we know about what the US is planning and how Iran could respond.

What new measures is the US threatening against Iran?

The Trump administration has already been waging an economic pressure campaign against Iran under the banner of “Operation Economic Fury”, since the launch of the war in February.

In particular, it is currently running a naval blockade on Iranian ports in a bid to prevent oil exports and has targeted companies, brokers and tankers accused of helping Iran sell its oil abroad.

It also has longer standing sweeping sanctions in place on Iran’s oil, shipping and financial sectors, seeking to cut off the revenue Tehran earns from energy exports. It has also imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports.

In a Truth Social post on Wednesday, Trump announced what he called the “most crushing economic operation” against Iran.

Trump said Iran had “failed to take” the opportunity to make a deal, and would face “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale”.

He also threatened sanctions against any country that does business with Iran.

“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” he wrote.

“Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies – it all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are. This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat.”

On Thursday last week, one day after Trump’s social media tirade, Bessent told the news service CNBC that the US would apply the “toughest sanctions in history” on Iran.

“It is a one-two punch. We have the blockade [on Iran], and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” Bessent said. “It is going to work in Iran, and we are going to collapse this regime.”

He then offered a warning to the members of the international community that they, too, could face economic penalties if they continue to trade with Iran.

“We’re going to them and saying: You’re either with us or against us,” Bessent said. “If you insist on doing business with them – either transferring money, buying oil, doing seaborne ship transport – then the US Treasury and the US government, they will put its full might and force towards enforcing against you.”

He billed the US’s strategy as the “greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world”.

“It is time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision,” Bessent added.

Iran has decried any new, impending US sanctions – particularly economic action against other countries – as a “complete erosion of sovereignty”.

In a post on X on Saturday, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said the US announcement was “an assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty” against the United Nations’ member states.

No state can compel foreign banks, enterprises or airports to renounce commerce with Iran, he said.

“The end result would be the complete erosion of sovereignty as the foundational basis of the UN-based inter-State system, and a recipe for an abysmal return to full-scale classic colonialism,” Baghaei said.

Iranian state media pointed out that Tehran has faced US sanctions for decades. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the new measures were “bound to fail”.

“We have seen this movie before,” Araghchi wrote on X, alongside a screenshot of a tweet from former President Barack Obama referencing earlier sanctions in 2012. “Same bull. Different bullies.”

Can Iran target countries that acquiesce to US demands?

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told the IRIB state broadcaster that Iran was appealing to all countries around the world, including its neighbours, not to join the US’s “economic war”.

“Any country that takes part in imposing economic restrictions on us will be regarded as an enemy,” he said, warning of a “seismic” retaliation.

Rezaei described Iran’s strategy as a three-stage sequence starting with talks to de-escalate tensions.

“Of course, we will first negotiate with them. We will hold talks and tell them to step aside and distance themselves from the United States. But if they do not act, we will strike. We will target that country’s interests,” he said.

Rezaei also warned Iran’s neighbours that if they participate in Trump’s economic warfare, “not even a drop of oil” will leave the Gulf region, including by alternative export routes away from the Hormuz chokepoint through which one-fifth of global oil and gas exports pass in peacetime.

Iran has already launched strikes on US military installations, infrastructure and civilian locations in the region since the war began on February 28.

Energy and other facilities in Qatar , Kuwait , Saudi Arabia , Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have also suffered damage, mostly from debris from intercepted strikes by Iran or its proxy groups across the region.

The US operates military facilities in more than a dozen locations across the Middle East and North Africa, including in Gulf nations, such as Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE. Thousands of US soldiers are also stationed across the region, including in Jordan.

Hamidreza Azizi, a researcher on Iran at the Clingendael Institute, said in a post on X on Saturday: “Tehran appears to be trying to establish deterrence at an earlier stage, by signalling that even preparations for an attack could trigger an Iranian response.”

Azizi said two elements in the new “offensive doctrine” are emerging: preemption, which is aimed at preventing a perceived threat from materialising; and disproportionate retaliation, which is aimed at raising the cost of any attack that does occur.

How have other countries responded to Trump’s demands?

China has pushed back against Trump’s threats.

“Imposing sanctions and pressuring do not help to solve the issue,” China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian told reporters in Beijing on August 20.

“China calls on relevant parties to take responsible measures and solve the issues through diplomatic and political means.”

Gulf countries, which are Iran’s neighbours and also US allies, have increasingly been finding themselves caught in the middle of the war. Therefore, it is unclear if they would all join Washington in economically threatening Iran further.

Last week, the UAE, on which Iran is believed to rely for critical imports and financial services through which it sells oil, announced an indefinite trade embargo on Iran, after accusing Iranian forces of firing two ballistic missiles at the country, an allegation Tehran denies.

However, analysts have told Al Jazeera that many Gulf states fear the chaos that could follow if Iran’s government were to collapse. They said that while regional confidence in diplomacy is low, no country can afford another long war.

“Ultimately, Gulf countries can’t change geography. They have to live and work alongside Iran,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera in an interview last month. “They don’t want the instability that would come from the fall of the Islamic Republic [of Iran]. I think some Gulf states have pushed for harder strikes – not to precipitate its collapse, but to weaken the more hardline elements of the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps].”

Can China and Russia insulate Iran from US measures?

While the US has made threats against any country that continues to trade with Iran, analysts say that Trump’s leverage over China and Russia , both major trading partners of Iran, is limited.

Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera last week that “it is going to be very difficult” for Trump to pull off his pressure campaign effectively.

“Trump is trying to unilaterally assert the kind of coordinated sanctions that traditionally has taken multilateral coordination, and that means getting on board China, Russia, the P5 of the UN Security Council,” Musgrave said, referring to the five permanent members of the UNSC.

This is because several sectors in Russia and China have minimal reliance on the American financial system.

Those sectors include most of China’s oil refineries . According to analytics firm Kpler, China bought 80 percent of Iran’s shipped oil in 2025. Evidence of ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian oil off the coast of Malaysia has also shown how Iranian oil continues to be traded.

Analysts say China could also hit back if the US sanctions the major Chinese banks for processing Iranian funds, as the US Treasury has threatened .

“Trump intends to stabilise the ties with China, so [this would happen] as Beijing aims to have a temporary truce with Washington,” Yu Jie, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House think tank’s China, Asia Pacific Programme, told Al Jazeera.

Although Russia is a less significant trading partner for Iran than China, Moscow and Tehran have spent years developing critical commercial and military links designed to sidestep Western channels. Notably, Iran has provided Shahed drones to Moscow for use in its war on Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia's second-biggest online retailer Ozon targeted in Ukrainian strikes
articles.summary: Ozon says its warehouses across southern Russia, including in Dagestan and Krasnodar, were hit in the overnight strikes.
articles.body:
Warehouses belonging to Russia's second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes.

Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes.

Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv's "most sensitive economic sectors".

Russia has targeted Ukraine's civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals.

Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.

Ozon said "a fire broke out" at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday.

The company said earlier that a "major fire" was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site.

Russia's defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia's children's rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital.

Russia's businesses under strain from Ukraine's attacks on Wildberries

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv

Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated.

Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan.

Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%.

When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was "working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation".

The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon's site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured.

Following that strike, Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday: "Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy's logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole.

"After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon's turn."

Meanwhile, in Ukraine's Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region's head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram.

Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia's first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country.

Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points.

The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians.

Both companies have been described as "Russia's Amazon" and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population.

In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances.

But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments.

This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses.

The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies.

articles.title: India used pellets, grenades on Gen Z protests: What Amnesty report reveals
articles.summary: Security forces used tear gas, pellet guns and electric shock devices against student protesters, Amnesty inquiry found.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – An investigation by human rights group Amnesty International has confirmed that Indian government forces used lethal weapons, including pellet-firing shotguns, grenades, batons and electric shock devices against demonstrators in Gen Z protests that rocked the national capital last month.

On July 20, thousands of protesters had all but shut down New Delhi, blocking off Parliament Street, demanding the resignation of then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan following a string of examination scandals involving the leaking of national exam papers and other irregularities.

More than 100 students were injured in the crackdown by police and paramilitary forces that day. Indian newspapers obtained hospital records that showed that doctors had treated pellet wounds in several cases.

India’s opposition, led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi, has since called on Home Minister Amit Shah, seen as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s confidant, to answer questions about the alleged police brutality and has joined protesters in calling for his resignation.

But despite mounting evidence and growing political criticism, the Modi government repeatedly insisted that security forces had been measured in their response to the protests and denied using excessive force.

Now, an Amnesty investigation has found the use of tactics that Indian law enforcement rulebooks themselves warn against using in all but exceptional circumstances.

In July, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a satirical, youth-led movement which gathered momentum in response to the national examinations scandal, called on its supporters to march on the Indian Parliament after a monthlong sit-in failed to oust the education minister.

Two days before the march, the police forcibly removed renowned activist Sonam Wangchuk, who had been taking part in a hunger strike. That move galvanised public anger, bringing out more protesters in New Delhi.

On the morning of the march day, the police used tear gas as protesters swelled, then attacked them with electric shock batons, as well as shooting at them with pellet guns, Amnesty International’s Evidence Lab has verified from video and photographic evidence alongside witness testimony.

Amnesty also found that government forces had put up barricades and enforced a communications blackout.

“The weapons were deployed in a manner that breached international law and standards and domestic policing guidelines,” Amnesty said in a statement on Monday.

The rights group’s report also noted that the Delhi Police had publicly denied any disproportionate use of force, specifically pellet guns. The police also repeated this before India’s top court during a hearing about the alleged use of excessive force.

Amnesty says the evidence it has gathered “directly contradicts [the police’s] account”.

Four days after the July 20 march, as protests spread across the country, police in Bihar state’s Siwan town opened fire on protesters, injuring at least three youths.

Did government forces fire pellets at protesters?

Following the July 20 protest, several videos and photos emerged of protesters with injuries consistent with pellet wounds, which were reflected in their medical records as well.

The Evidence Lab verified two videos showing a paramilitary Rapid Action Force officer firing a shotgun into the crowd at the intersection of Connaught Place and Parliament Street in New Delhi, where protesters had gathered.

At least two protesters had wounds consistent with those caused by birdshot, a hunting round that fires a large number of small metal pellets, the group noted.

“The doctors confirmed that they were pellet injuries. Thankfully, my bones have been saved, but my body has been scarred badly,” one protester told Amnesty.

Amnesty said birdshot ammunition has not been developed for law enforcement purposes due to the widespread dispersion of the metal pellets, which “is inherently inaccurate and presents a high risk of serious injuries to the targeted person and even bystanders”.

Amnesty also said the police did not issue a public warning before firing pellet guns, as recommended by the Indian government’s Bureau for Police Research and Development.

Police and security forces have used metal pellets for more than a decade in Indian-administered Kashmir, leading to the first mass blinding during a 2016 civilian uprising.

Posting on X, Delhi Police called the reports of pellet injuries during the latest protests “fake news”, “completely false and misleading” and warned that “appropriate legal action” would be taken against anyone “spreading rumours”.

A subsequent internal inquiry by India’s paramilitary forces, however, reportedly found that personnel had fired at least seven rounds of ammunition containing metal pellets.

“Instead of facilitating the right to protest, Indian authorities suppressed it first with a communication blackout, barricades and transport disruption. They then attempted to crush it with unnecessary or excessive use of force against peaceful protesters, including children,” said Aakar Patel, chair of the board, Amnesty International India.

“This heavy-handed response was state-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control. The continued impunity after a month is a testament to that,” Patel said.

Did police use tear gas grenades and batons?

Government forces did use tear gas grenades to disperse the crowd at several places in New Delhi, as seen by Al Jazeera and verified by Amnesty, not just on July 20 to prevent CHP supporters’ march to Parliament.

“Tear gas grenades releasing an excessive amount of explosive energy are extremely dangerous and should be prohibited for use in public assemblies,” Amnesty said, referring to videos of tear gas shells exploding near students.

The group also noted that witnesses observed that “tear gas grenades were launched directly at protesters instead of at an angled trajectory above the head of protesters, at odds with UN Guidance on the use of Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement”.

Amnesty has also verified claims that the police used lathis, the Indian version of batons, to beat protesters.

The UN special rapporteur on torture considers lathis to be inherently cruel, inhuman or degrading as “they deliver a greater level [of] kinetic force than conventional batons, causing excessive pain and increasing the risk of serious injury” and has called for them to be prohibited, a position that Amnesty supports.

The group also found men in civilian clothing beating protesters “while uniformed officers, who escorted them toward the crowd, stand beside them and make no attempt to intervene”, as visible in videos seen by Al Jazeera. Several officials were not wearing their name tags or badge numbers, as required.

What has been the reaction to the use of excessive force?

A day after the crackdown in New Delhi, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke told the crowd, “Every police person who attacked you would be identified and dragged to the courts”.

The group also launched a platform for protesters to upload videos and photos from the crackdown.

The opposition, led by the Congress’s Gandhi, pushed the home minister for a discussion on the issue in Parliament, an issue that plagued the monsoon session with Shah missing.

Gandhi argued that either Shah ordered the usage of lethal weapons, in which case “he is guilty”, or he was unaware of the situation, which makes him “incompetent” for the job.

Sahil Lochab, a 19-year-old who lost vision in one eye due to pellet injuries, said the police had been refusing to register his complaint. In response, Gandhi staged a seven-hour sit-in outside the office of the Delhi Police chief, insisting that a case be registered over the use of pellet guns on protesters, alongside Lochab.

After Gandhi’s pressure, the police relented. A student at the University of Delhi, Lochab received multiple pellet injuries on his chest, back, arms and face. Several pellets could not be taken out, he said in his complaint.

“My medical documents show that there are over 200 pellets in my body. Doctors have told me that the possibility of my eyesight coming back is less than 1 percent,” Lochab wrote in his complaint.

articles.title: Dutch broadcaster Avrotros pulls out of  2027 Eurovision Song Contest
articles.summary: It says contest can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.
articles.body:
Dutch public broadcaster Avrotros has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, saying that the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict.

In a statement released on Monday, the broadcaster said the decision was due to a lack of clarity from organisers - the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) - over assessing which countries could compete.

Avrotros added: "The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years."

Earlier this month, the EBU updated its rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year. But Avrotros said those changes "do not provide sufficient confidence that ‌the ⁠independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored".

The broadcaster's withdrawal from next year's contest in Burgas, Bulgaria, does not necessarily rule out Dutch participation.

Another public broadcaster could potentially take it on as the country has several.

Avrotros pulled out of this year's event in Vienna, Austria, which the Netherlands also boycotted after Israel were allowed to compete.

Only Ireland - who also pulled out of this year's event - and Sweden have won Eurovision more than the Netherlands.

Martin Green, director of the contest, said in a statement that the EBU regretted Avrotros's decision but respected its views.

"We will now continue our dialogue with NPO, the umbrella organisation for Dutch public service media, regarding the opportunities for another broadcaster to participate. We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest."

Taco Zimmerman, director general of Avrotos, said the Eurovision Song Contest "was originally created to bring people and countries together" but was now "a platform for division".

He said: "It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character.

"The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division. As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values."

He added: "They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts. That is painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the contest again next year."

Green, however, stated that the contest "has always been a place to bring people together, celebrate diverse communities, and show that a better world is possible even in the most difficult times".

The NPO said it was "very sorry" to hear that one of its broadcasters had pulled out of Eurovision again, but added that "we respect Avrotros's decision".

"We also recognise that the geopolitical tensions are having a divisive effect," it responded.

"That's why this hasn't been an easy decision for our colleagues. We will reflect on the upcoming edition and will come back to this at the right moment."

The organisation concluded it was "too early to comment on the next steps at this point" and that its members were "currently deliberating on that".

The recent amendment to the rules, that mean a country involved in an armed military conflict can't host the next contest if it wins, was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026.

It stated that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region".

Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain, Ireland and the Netherlands.

Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle.

It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future.

Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022.

Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support.

articles.title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
articles.summary: Job site Adzuna said the number of graduate vacancies was the lowest since 2016
articles.body:
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.

Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.

Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.

However, some have said the data might not be reflective of the whole graduate job market and may instead suggest a shift in the way the roles are advertised.

Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.

The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.

Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.

But graduate jobs expert Charlie Ball said the numbers might not be as bad for graduates as they first appear.

He said they could instead suggest that firms are advertising fewer roles specifically for graduates, even if the roles themselves still exist and end up being filled by graduates.

From his experience in the sector, Ball said the graduate market has "not collapsed" but added: "We know the graduate jobs market is weak. We know it's not in great shape."

Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million .

Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.

They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications .

Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.

The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.

But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities .

A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall.

"We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our £2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."

articles.title: Driven by progressive doomism, liberals are having fewer babies than conservative families
articles.summary: The fertility rate gap between conservatives and liberals reflects diverging priorities on family, career, and creative pursuits, new research suggests.
articles.body: America’s political divide is extending into the nursery, as data shows conservatives are having more children than liberals. The Atlantic, citing research from the Institute for Family Studies (IFS), reported that self-identified conservatives have an average of 1.4 children, compared to 1.09 for liberals. It’s a gap IFS researchers said remained even after controlling for other variables, such as sex, religion, race, income, age, marital status and education. "Having children — particularly lots of children — has become a bit right-coded, as the kids say. Americans and Europeans who identify as leftist or liberal tend to have fewer children than those who identify as conservative or right-leaning," Atlantic staff writer Olga Khazan wrote in her article, "Another Big Difference Between Liberals and Conservatives." FORMER NEBRASKA SENATOR BATTLING CANCER WARNS PEOPLE HAVE 'STOPPED MAKING BABIES' The Trump administration has positioned itself as pro-family, with prominent members, including Vice President JD Vance, urging the country to have more babies.  The administration has also proposed financial incentives aimed at raising the birthrate, including a $5,000 "baby bonus" for mothers giving birth, while Trump signed an executive order expanding access to in vitro fertilization (IVF). Khazan argues that research shows that the birthrate divide between parties may have more to do with lifestyle choices and different priorities between the two groups. She argues that conservatives are more likely to view family as vital to a fulfilled life, while liberals may place greater emphasis on higher education, creative pursuits or career success. "In one recent Pew Research Center poll, for instance, Republicans were more likely than Democrats to say that having children was ‘highly important’ for living a fulfilling life, and in another, Democrats were more likely than Republicans to say that creative activities were ‘one of the most important things’ to them," Khazan said. "Democrats, then, may be less willing to choose parenthood when it competes as a priority with career, friendships, travel, and other pursuits," she added. The article also suggested that liberal anxiety extends beyond daily stress to include systemic worries over climate change, reproductive healthcare access and therapy-driven fears of repeating family trauma. TRUMP BEAT BACK ANTI-FAMILY TAXES IN 2025. HERE’S WHAT NEEDS TO HAPPEN NEXT The Institute for Family Studies research also found that liberals report significantly higher levels of concern about parenting and their mental health.  Ken Burchfiel, an IFS research fellow who worked on the study, told Fox News Digital that where Democrats live could also help explain the difference. "We found that partisan differences in parenting attitudes held up even when controlling for age, sex, race, household income, relationship status, education, religion, and parental status. That means that these differences aren't merely a result of diverging faith preferences or income gaps," Burchfiel said. "The question remains, then: what is driving this change? My hypothesis is that Democrats' tendency to live in more urban areas may help explain these gaps. If you live in a small apartment in a major city, you probably are more likely to see parenting as very stressful and difficult; after all, raising a child is more expensive and complicated in the heart of an urban area than in the suburbs," he added. Burchfiel also suggested that adults in major urban centers may have fewer daily opportunities to interact with parents and children, potentially leaving them less confident about starting families of their own. AMERICA’S BABY BUST MAY BE LINKED TO THE IPHONE, STUDY SAYS "As a result, you might feel less confident about your own ability to be a parent. Such opportunities might continue to decline now that major cities are experiencing a drop in the numbers of children," Burchfiel added. Overall, the number of births in the United States and the general fertility rate have decreased, according to the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics. articles.title: Salisbury artists create music and murals for River Park trail
articles.summary: The trail in Salisbury celebrates the history of the area and highlights local wildlife.
articles.body:
Artists have come together to create music and murals as part of a new nature trail.

The Salisbury River Park's Artwork Trail, in Wiltshire, has been created to celebrate the history of the area and highlight the local wildlife which calls the green space home.

Spots on the trail include fish-inspired picnic benches by local artist Zac Newham, a dragonfly sculpture by Jane Edden and drawings by illustrator Francesca McLean.

Clare Christopher, from Studio Response, which was involved in the project, said each artist brought "their own distinct voice" to the trail "while responding to the shared themes of nature, community and place that define the River Park".

'Alcohol ruled my life – now my eyes are open'

Historic windmill transformed with new sails

Fire that damaged allotments thought to be arson

The Salisbury River Park is a £45m green corridor of public open space which runs alongside the river Avon. It was built to deliver flood risk mitigation for the city.

Christopher added: "The trail offers a gentle, inviting way for people to experience the artworks, encouraging people to move through the River Park at their own pace, notice the details of the landscape and enjoy the artworks in relation to the river environment around them."

A trail map has been created which links each piece of art, with a version available for children.

Other artwork includes a mural by Fred Fieber on the coach park toilet block and Tech Moon's mural on the central car park toilet block which celebrates animals that can be found in the area including Atlantic Salmon and European Otter.

Composer Karen Wimhurst has contributed eight musical pieces inspired by the River Park and the neighbouring Avon Valley Nature Reserve, which can be listened to along the trail.

The project was curated by public art commissioning organisation Studio Response, in partnership with Salisbury City Council. The map has been released by the Environment Agency (EA).

Andy Wallis, Salisbury River Park project lead at the EA, said the trail was created to "reconnect people with the rivers that flow through their city."

He added: "Each piece encourages visitors to look more closely at the wildlife and natural heritage found along our chalk streams, from the delicate wings of a mayfly to the otters and kingfishers that call this place home."

articles.title: Firefighters make progress against Reno, Nevada, wildfire that’s destroyed over 30 homes
articles.summary: At least six people — three first responders and three civilians — were injured. Officials said the fire was “human-caused” but didn’t provide details about how they reached that conclusion or whether it was intentionally set or accidental.
articles.body: RENO, Nevada — Crews have started to contain a wildfire in the Sierra Nevada foothills near Reno, Nevada, that destroyed more than 30 homes as it spread perilously close to dense neighborhoods, officials said Monday. Containment reached 27% and there was no new growth of the Hawk Fire, which has held steady at about 23 square miles since it burned out of control on Sunday, authorities said at an afternoon news briefing. “We are making progress,” said U.S. Forest Service District Ranger Matt Zumstein. The number of residents under evacuation orders and warnings was reduced to about 63,000, down from more than 90,000 people when the blaze mushroomed over the weekend. While winds have eased, there’s still concern that gusts could push the flames through dry brush into newly developed neighborhoods in Nevada’s largest city outside of metro Las Vegas. Firefighters are also contending with hot temperatures and low humidity. At least 32 homes have burned and six are damaged, but authorities said those numbers are sure to rise as assessment teams begin to survey the charred areas. Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve said the way the fire spread so quickly at its height had her fearing for the worst. “It lit up these areas like nothing I’ve seen before,” she said Monday. “It took your breath away, in the worst way.” Hawk Fire triggers evacuations and school closures Schools across Washoe County were closed Monday because of the evacuations and to keep roads clear for emergency crews. Nevada’s governor declared a state of emergency in the county and mobilized the National Guard to help with aerial firefighting and protecting evacuated neighborhoods northwest of downtown Reno. At one roadblock, residents expressed frustration Monday that they could not get back into their homes. “There’s no fire here! Why are the National Guard here?” a driver yelled. Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said he understands that some residents are frustrated that they can’t get home, but the danger isn’t over yet. “It just takes that little breeze and one ember,” he said. Wildfires near Reno are blamed on human activity The fire near the California state line began Saturday and exploded in size on Sunday. At least seven people — three first responders and four civilians — have been injured. This is the third large wildfire in the rugged terrain north of Reno in the past two weeks — all caused by human activity, according to fire officials. They haven’t said whether the Hawk Fire was intentionally set or accidental. Much of the area that burned was sagebrush and grass. Reno, home to about 280,000 people, is known for its casinos and as a gateway to nearby Lake Tahoe, North America’s largest alpine lake and a popular vacation destination. It’s also southwest of Nevada’s Black Rock Desert, site of the annual Burning Man festival, which begins next Sunday. Many who travel to Burning Man make Reno a regular stop. Organizers on Monday asked attendees to not take hotel rooms and other resources away from fire evacuees, while being mindful of closures. “Treat our neighbors, first responders, hospitality workers and everyone affected by this emergency with patience and care,” a Burning Man statement said. Fire claims a Reno woman’s home for a second time Videos posted on social media showed the smoldering ruins of homes and cars, with only a scorched basketball hoop still standing. Crystal Hallock, 53, lost her home to fire for a second time in less than a decade. She moved into the rebuilt house in 2019, a year after an electrical fire burned it down. On Saturday, with a giant plume of smoke and flames visible on the nearby mountaintop, she fled with her children, grandchildren and pets. Her ex-husband tried to save the property and her vintage Cadillac, grabbing a garden hose as flames melted children’s toys and burned bushes. She urged him over the phone to get out and feared the worst when the line went dead. “He was saying he can’t breathe, it’s so dark I can’t see, and I’m screaming at him, ‘Leave the car, just leave it,’” she said Monday. Thirty minutes later, he called to say he had gotten out with the car. “I’m truly blessed because I have a place to stay with my animals and my grandkids. We were all able to get out safely,” she said from a niece’s apartment in Reno. Nevada fire spread quickly in foothills Many residents had little time to evacuate after the fire exploded in size. “Honestly, I thought it was like in a movie,” said Ruby Delatorre, who got back from a concert only to find her home in the evacuation zone. She returned Sunday to walk to her house and get a few more possessions. “I literally want to cry and go back for all my stuff. I just got what I thought I needed,” Delatorre said. Some who spotted the smoke on Saturday thought it was from another wildfire that has been burning the past two weeks. “The flames were pretty close to my house, and the smoke was really thick, but we have no idea if our house survived or not,” Jon Hanbury said Monday at Reno’s convention center, which is now a shelter. Wildfire threat remains high in the West Much of Nevada’s western edge is under an increased risk of wildfires this week because of high winds and low relative humidity, the National Interagency Fire Center said. The National Weather Service says the region will see warm, dry and breezy conditions, and that critical fire weather conditions are possible in the week’s later half. Reno sits at an elevation of 4,500 feet. Extremely dry conditions across the American West have sparked a rash of wildfires this summer. Fires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area in early August. Nationwide, there have been more than 50,000 wildfires — the most over the past 10 years covering the same time period, according to the national fire center.

articles.title: Bessent doubles down on Trump warnings: ‘Entering the endgame’ on Iran
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday previewed the Trump administration’s economic offensive against Iran, set to begin Monday. Echoing President Trump’s rhetoric on the military operations against the Islamic Republic, Bessent said the U.S. has “dismantled Iran’s capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program.” The Treasury secretary wrote…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday previewed the Trump administration’s economic offensive against Iran, set to begin Monday.

Echoing President Trump’s rhetoric on the military operations against the Islamic Republic , Bessent said the U.S. has “dismantled Iran’s capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear program.”

The Treasury secretary wrote on social media , “We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.”

Bessent is expected to address the looming sanctions in a press conference Monday afternoon.

Trump said last week his administration will undertake a “CRUSHING” economic operation against Iran, equating it to “Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale.”

In a post on Truth Social , the president warned other countries that allowing their “financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran” would result in economic consequences.

In conjunction with the military strikes against Iran, the Treasury Department has targeted the regime financially via its “ Operation Economic Fury ” initiative.

Among other actions, the department has frozen Iranian assets around the world, cracked down on the regime’s shadow banking networks and sanctioned the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, which the Iranian government created to handle shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

On Sunday, Bessent said the latest economic operation will “leverage every agency, every authority and action many assumed we would never summon.”

He added, “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains the tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”

In advance of the economic operation from Washington, Iran’s rial currency dipped to a record-low 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar early Monday morning, The Associated Press reported.

articles.title: Ancient clue cracks open a 2,000-year-old mystery near famed Colosseum
articles.summary: Archaeologists working near Rome's Colosseum uncovered eight rooms with mosaics and painted decorations that may belong to an ancient Roman firehouse.
articles.body: Archaeologists digging near Rome's Colosseum believe they may have found an ancient firehouse dating back nearly 2,000 years. The building, which dates to the second century A.D., was found in the Villa Celimontana park near the Colosseum, Reuters reported this month. Villa Celimontana dates to the 16th century, when it was developed as a noble residence on Caelian Hill, one of the seven hills of ancient Rome. CONSTRUCTION WORKERS CLEARING OLD BOMBS UNEXPECTEDLY FIND 'IMPORTANT' ANCIENT SANCTUARY The discovery was originally announced by Rome's archaeological superintendency, part of Italy's Ministry of Culture. At the excavation site, archaeologists fully uncovered five of the building's eight rooms, which contain mosaics and remnants of painted decorations. Officials believe the building may have been part of the nearby barracks of the Fifth Cohort of the Vigiles, ancient Rome's firefighting force. They cited one telling clue: A mosaic found at the site closely resembles one previously discovered in a firefighters' barracks in Ostia, ancient Rome's port city. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER SPRAWLING ROMAN ESTATE BURIED FOR CENTURIES BENEATH FARMLAND The Vigiles were also tasked with maintaining public order at night, and their nearby barracks used water from an aqueduct. "If this hypothesis is confirmed, the discovery would help reassess the extent of one of the most important military complexes of imperial Rome," officials said in a statement. Pictures show the remains of the ancient building, including exposed walls and sections uncovered during the excavation. Other images show fragments of mosaic uncovered at the site. The elaborate decorations could support that hypothesis, officials said. The possible firehouse is the latest in a string of ancient Roman discoveries to emerge across Italy in recent months. articles.title: Tropical Storm Moke set to dump more heavy rain on hurricane-stricken Hawaii
articles.summary: HONOLULU — Tropical Storm Moke was swirling past Hawaii on Sunday, close enough to dump heavy rain on Big Island communities in the aftermath of Hurricane Lala.
articles.body: HONOLULU — Tropical Storm Moke was swirling past Hawaii on Sunday, close enough to dump heavy rain on Big Island communities in the aftermath of Hurricane Lala. The National Hurricane Center located Moke’s center about 320 miles south-southwest of Hilo around midday. Top sustained winds were around 40 mph, though the real impact was expected from rainfall in places where last weekend’s hurricane flooded communities, triggered mudslides and damaged roads and power lines. Two deaths linked to the hurricane have been reported in Hawaii. Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda advised residents in a social media post Sunday they “should stay off the roads and shelter in place” as a precaution. He said anyone in need could take refuge at shelters that the county had opened at several locations. Forecasters expected Moke to produce as much as 10 inches of total rain across the Big Island, and up to 15 inches in some isolated places, enough to cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides for the windward and southeast slopes, especially in steep terrain and over areas affected by Lala. The center of the storm was expected to pass south of the Big Island, then south of the smaller main islands of Hawaii. In eastern Maui, up to 6 inches of rain was expected, and the other islands may get an inch or two, according to the hurricane center. As with Hurricane Lala, the Big Island was expected to bear the brunt of Moke’s rain and winds as the storm moves westward, south of the island chain. After moving away from the islands, Lala was downgraded and remained a strong tropical storm on Sunday far out in the Central Pacific. The northeast coast of the Big Island saw the heaviest total rainfall from Lala, at 43.54 inches, according to the weather service. Ahead of Moke’s approach, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green urged people to prepare by restocking food, medicine and other essentials. More than 6,500 customers in the county remained without power Sunday stemming from Lala, according to poweroutage.us. In the eastern Pacific, meanwhile, Tropical Storm Iselle formed earlier Sunday and was gaining strength, far away from Mexico’s southwest coast. Iselle had top sustained winds of 50 mph Sunday afternoon and was about 535 miles southwest of the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect for Iselle as it moved to the northwest at 16 mph. The U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said Iselle could become a hurricane in another day or two and would kick up strong ocean swells on Baja’s western coastline starting Monday.

articles.title: UK missiles offer may help Ukraine - but they are not what Zelensky needs most
articles.summary: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham is handing over blueprints so Kyiv can build its own long-range missiles.
articles.body:
The UK is set to hand over blueprints for its British-French designed Storm Shadow cruise missiles to Ukraine – following a similar move from France – allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

The move sends an important signal, showing that some Western nations are willing to share their expertise and know how to help Ukraine defend itself.

But, on its own, this won't dramatically alter the course of the war.

Scalp and Storm Shadow missiles have already been provided to Kyiv by both Britain and France. They've already been used to hit military targets inside Russia.

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv Published 1 day ago

Burnham to hand long-range missile blueprints to Zelensky as he visits Kyiv

The weapons are not new – they were developed in the 1990s - and they are expensive – at around £1m a piece.

They also rely on complex global supply chains and have been built in peacetime at relatively low rates – in the hundreds, not the thousands.

Even with the blueprints, Ukraine may find it hard to source components. It could take months, possibly years to make the cruise missile themselves.

Copying Western weapons production in peacetime is, in fact, no way to win a war. Even Nato nations now realise that.

Britain and many of its allies have tended to produce small quantities of highly advanced, expensive missiles which would quickly run out in any protracted conflict.

In 2021, the former head of the US Army in Europe, Gen Ben Hodges, said that in a Nato wargame the UK military ran out of key weapons within a matter of days.

Proof of the recent change in mindset is the UK military is no longer buying Storm Shadow missiles for itself.

Instead, under Project Brakestop, it is developing its own long-range cruise missiles, free of foreign components, and less than half the price of a Storm Shadow.

Project Brakestop is also being done at break-neck speed. The UK hopes to have a new cruise missile ready by the end of the year. It is promising to supply the new weapon to Ukraine.

It is Ukraine which has shown the world how to produce relatively cheap, mass produced weapons, necessary for a long, protracted conflict.

Douglas Barrie, Senior Fellow for Military Aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) told the BBC: "The decision to share UK classified information on the MBDA SCALP missiles with Ukraine, as France and Ukraine work toward local assembly lines in Ukraine, is notable. Any impact, however, will in part depend on how quickly Ukrainian assembled SCALP cruise missiles can be introduced into service.

"Given that Ukraine has already operated both Storm Shadow and SCALP, familiarity with the missile may help speed the overall process, but this will also be dependent on the extent and pace at which local assembly can be established."

At the start of the war its armed forces relied on old Cold War-era Soviet weaponry.

A slow supply of Western weapons helped it adapt. But now Ukraine produces 70% of its own weapons.

Key has been its rapid development of drone technology – from small First Person View (FPV) one-way attack drones for the front line, to larger long-range drones capable of striking deep into Russian territory, further than Storm Shadows can strike.

Kyiv is on track to build 10 million drones by the end of this year. And they can do it cheaper than the West, by using mass-produced Chinese parts.

Nato allies' equivalent drones can be twice as expensive as they try to shun Chinese components.

However, there are still weapons that Ukraine needs and struggles to produce on its own. From fast fighter jets to the most urgent example, interceptors to take down Russian ballistic missiles

The most effective weapon to do that, by far, is the US-made Patriot interceptor. Ukraine has all but run out of them and Russian ballistic missiles now make it through Ukrainian air defences with ease.

America's war in Iran has meant they're in even shorter supply.

They're also expensive – at around £3m a missile – and production rates have been slow. The US is planning to double production rates from around 600 Patriot missiles per annum to 2,000, but that will take several years.

President Donald Trump signalled last month that he would be willing to share Patriot technology with Ukraine, but has since rowed back .

Even if he had given approval, it would have taken a while for Ukraine to make Patriots themselves - some estimate at least a year. Ukraine would also be relying on the same sophisticated components that are in high demand across the globe.

Ukraine has embarked on a programme to develop its own interceptor missiles with European support – known as Project Freya.

But there are huge technological challenges in building a high-speed missile to take down another missile travelling at thousands of miles per hour. It is expensive and often time consuming.

Ukraine's military and its weapons manufacturers have shown themselves to be fast learners.

One of its own companies, Fire Point, is developing its own ballistic missiles which it hopes will be ready to fire in anger next year.

But Russia has already ramped up its own ballistic missile production, to around 100 a month.

Developing sophisticated weapons is expensive and cannot be done quickly. Ukraine is short of both time and money.

So, the move to hand missile blueprints to Ukraine will be welcome, but it is not an immediate fix for Ukraine's most pressing problems, and it wwill not dramatically alter Kyiv's ability to strike Russia in new ways.

articles.title: New Zealand moves to ban children under 16 from social media
articles.summary: The government faces opposition to its proposals from MPs who believe a ban will not work.
articles.body:
New Zealand is to introduce a bill seeking to ban under-16s from using social media.

Under the latest proposals, platforms including TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and Facebook, will have to take steps to check users are over 16 and platforms that fail to meet their obligations could face fines of up to 10% of their global revenue.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media was exposing children to "harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with". But several political parties have said they will vote against the bill.

The move follows a similar ban in Australia, while countries including the UK and Greece are set to introduce restrictions next year.

Luxon said social media was affecting children's family life, mental health, sleep and education.

"We have protections to keep children safe in the real world and we need them in the virtual world too," he said.

New Zealand's government has not outlined which other "high risk" platforms could be impacted.

A statement said that under the Online Safety Bill, which is being introduced to parliament on Monday, social media companies would be required to "take reasonable steps" to check users are over the age of 16 by using methods including existing account information, facial age estimation and digital identity checks.

Platforms regularly used by children would also be required to regularly assess the risks they pose and report on how they are being identified and reduced.

No penalties are proposed for children, parents or caregivers for breaches of the ban, but fines for social media companies could be substantially higher than in Australia, where the maximum penalty is $99m (£51.7m) .

It is unclear if the bill will get enough votes to pass however, after both the Act and New Zealand First (NZF) parties - which are coalition partners in the government - said they would oppose it.

David Seymour, New Zealand's deputy prime minister and leader of Act, said the ban would not work.

Foreign affairs minister Winston Peters, who leads the NZF party, said: "We have been concerned with the proposed legislation and the direction and slippery slope that legislation like this will inevitably take our country."

Peters also described a ban introduced in Australia in December as a "colossal failure".

The ban has been difficult for Australia to enforce, and it has been widely acknowledged that many children under the age of 16 have still been able to access and use banned apps.

Earlier this month, France's top court struck down a similar proposed social media ban, saying it infringed upon freedom of expression.

articles.title: The Danube has fallen so low that a 1,600-year-old Roman bridge is emerging from the river, revealing a piece of history hidden underwater for centuries
articles.summary: Europe News: For centuries the waters of the Danube, Europe's second-longest river, have concealed the remains of a remarkable Roman engineering feat. The river is.
articles.body: For centuries the waters of the Danube, Europe's second-longest river, have concealed the remains of a remarkable Roman engineering feat. The river is currently at extremely low levels, and parts of a 1,600-year-old bridge are emerging from the water, giving archaeologists a rare glimpse of a structure that has been largely concealed for centuries, states a Reuters report. According to the same report, the visible remains belong to the Constantine Bridge, one of the most ambitious bridges built in the Roman Empire. Archaeologists in Bulgaria are making use of the unusual conditions to record sections of the ancient building before the rising water levels hide them once again. Scroll down to read the details of the findings.An emperor's BridgeIf we go by the online reports, the bridge was built on the order of the Roman emperor Constantine I and opened in AD 328. Sucidava, on the other side of the Danube in present-day Romania, was linked to it, and to the ancient city of Ulpia Oescus in modern northern Bulgaria. The bridge was over 2 kilometers long and a remarkable feat of engineering in ancient times. It is considered one of the longest bridges of the ancient world, but it did not last very long. Historical evidence indicates that a large part of the bridge was destroyed around A.D. 367, and its remains lie beneath the Danube.Drought shows hidden foundationsA series of record-breaking heatwaves across Europe this summer has contributed to severe drought in parts of the continent, states Reuters. Major waterways like the Danube and Rhine are experiencing unusually dry conditions. The water level has fallen, exposing parts of the foundations of the Constantine Bridge near the village of Gigen in northern Bulgaria. The brief exposure offered archaeologists a rare chance to study the remains in their natural setting. âNature for some time exposes an object which is hidden under the Danube most of the time,â said Pavel Popov from the Regional Historical Museum in Pleven, describing the conditions as especially valuable for archaeological research to Reuters.Ancient ruins as seen by dronesRecently, a team from the Pleven museum visited the site to document the newly exposed remains. The exposed foundations were mapped by the researchers, who followed the line of the remaining structures, assessed their current state, and photographed them with drones. Aerial imagery enabled archaeologists to record details that would be difficult to capture from the riverside or water level. It is reported that the documentation would help researchers better understand the construction, layout, and surviving remains of the bridge.A rare glimpse of Roman engineeringThe Constantine Bridge is more than a spectacular find in archaeology. Its brief appearance is a rare opportunity for researchers to study an ancient structure normally buried beneath the Danube. Eventually the water levels will rise again and much of the bridge will be out of sight. But the photographs, maps and measurements made during this period could retain important facts about one of the Roman Empireâs most impressive engineering achievements.For now, the Danube has retreated, offering a brief glimpse of the past and revealing a bridge built almost 1,600 years ago that has emerged from the river that hid it, allowing modern researchers to reconnect with a remarkable chapter of Roman history.Image Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: South Korea says US cancelled upcoming joint marine exercises over Iran war
articles.summary: The cancellation follows Trump’s surprise order last week to scale back a separate annual joint military drill.
articles.body:
South Korea says the United States has cancelled a large joint amphibious landing exercise scheduled for next month due to constraints on force availability caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.

“The US Marine Corps formally notified our forces in June that its ability to deploy forces during this year’s Ssangyong exercise would be constrained due to the situation in the Middle East,” Han Seung-jeon, a spokesman for the South Korean Marine Corps, told reporters at a news briefing on Monday.

The biennial Ssangyong drills involve marine forces from South Korea and the US and are designed to strengthen combined operations, typically involving warships, aircraft and ground forces rehearsing amphibious landings.

Seoul and Washington were continuing consultations on resuming the amphibious exercise, the spokesman said, without giving details.

There was no immediate comment from the Pentagon.

The announcement follows US President Donald Trump’s surprise order last week to scale back a separate annual joint military exercise that ended last Friday, citing the cost and Seoul’s refusal to take part in the war on Iran.

The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were cut from 11 days to five .

Trump has also sought to revive the relationship he developed with North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un during his first term.

He wrote on his Truth Social platform last week that the Ulchi Freedom Shield drills sent “a signal that was totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful”.

Despite the reduction of the exercises, North Korea fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles last week and issued a statement denouncing the drills .

North Korea has long condemned such joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion.

The US president also said last week that it was important to “get along” with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 “very powerful” nuclear weapons. Seoul estimates that North Korea has 80 to 120 such weapons.

Trump met Kim three times during his first term, but Pyongyang accelerated its nuclear programmes after their second summit in Hanoi in 2019 collapsed without an agreement on North Korea’s denuclearisation.

articles.title: Death of man who went overboard from cruise ship 'not suspicious'
articles.summary: The man's body was found after he was reported missing on Friday, when the vessel was off the east coast of Scotland
articles.body:
The death of a man whose body was recovered after going overboard from a cruise ship off the east coast of Scotland is not being treated as suspicious, police have confirmed.

The man was reported missing from Ambassador Cruise Lines vessel MS Ambition, about 36 nautical miles from Arbroath, at 08:35 on Friday.

His body was recovered later that day following a major multi-agency search.

The man's identity has not been released, but Police Scotland said his next of kin had been informed.

Coastguard aircraft from Prestwick and Carlisle were scrambled to assist in the search along with a commercial search and rescue helicopter.

Lifeboat crews from Anstruther and Broughty Ferry and Coastguard teams from Dundee, Arbroath and St Andrews also joined the operation.

The ship had been on its return journey to Dundee from a solar eclipse cruise, with stops in Iceland and the Faroe Islands, when the incident happened.

It docked in Lerwick before returning to the city on Friday.

The ship left Dundee to sail to Newcastle shortly after 18:00.

articles.title: âUK participating in Ukraine warâ: What triggered Russiaâs âoutrageous threatâ to Britain

articles.body: Russia has accused the UK of 'directly' participating in the war in Ukraine after London agreed to share classified information to help Kyiv develop its own long-range missiles. The move has drawn a sharp warning from Moscow, which said British military support was adding “fuel to the fire” and obstructing efforts towards a peace deal.The warning came as Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv on Monday for his first overseas trip since taking office. Burnham was expected to announce that Britain had authorised defence company MBDA to share previously classified information about British-made components used in the SCALP long-range cruise missile.The information could eventually allow Ukraine to develop and produce its own version of the weapon. SCALP is the French version of Britain’s Storm Shadow missile, with the two systems incorporating shared French and British technology. The move is part of wider British and French plans to establish long-range missile production in Ukraine.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow viewed the decision extremely negatively. He accused Britain of repeatedly taking steps that deepen its involvement in the conflict and prevent progress towards a negotiated settlement.“Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime. Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel to the fire and methodically and regularly hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process,” Peskov told reporters.Why Moscow is turning up the heatPeskov also warned that Russia was already working to locate facilities involved in producing long-range missiles and other military equipment. “The production sites of such missiles, the production sites of other military equipment” would be identified, he said, with Russian forces intent on destroying them.The latest warning follows an earlier threat from Moscow over Britain’s military assistance to Ukraine. Russia had warned London of unspecified “consequences” after reports that British-made drones had been used in long-range strikes against Russian territory for the first time.Britain has continued to expand its military backing for Kyiv. London has also agreed to support France in establishing assembly lines in Ukraine for long-range missiles, while previously allowing Ukraine to use British-made drones for attacks against Russian targets.Burnham rejected Moscow’s accusations and described Russia’s threats against Britain as “outrageous”. Speaking in Kyiv, he said Britain would maintain its support for Ukraine despite the Kremlin’s warnings.“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine.”He later challenged the Kremlin’s characterisation of British assistance during an interview. “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?”Burnham made the remarks as European leaders gathered in Kyiv to mark Ukraine’s Independence Day. He compared Ukraine’s struggle against Russia with Britain’s fight against Nazi Germany and said Europe owed a debt of gratitude to Ukrainians for resisting Moscow.“My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” Burnham said in a speech outside St Sophia Cathedral.The British prime minister also joined a conference call with leaders of the Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that have pledged to help guarantee Ukraine’s security in the event of a future truce with Russia. European Council President António Costa travelled to Kyiv alongside Burnham, while French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz were expected to participate remotely.The confrontation comes as Russia and Ukraine remain locked in an escalating campaign of long-range attacks. Kyiv has increasingly targeted Russian oil and logistics infrastructure with drones, while Moscow has continued missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities, infrastructure and military-related facilities.Ukraine has warned that Russia is building up its ballistic missile stockpile and considering the mobilisation of an additional 300,000 troops.
