articles.title: Netherlands: Sixteen injured as coach carrying German students and van collide
articles.summary: Eight people, including the driver of a delivery van, are seriously hurt, police say.
articles.body:
Sixteen people have been injured as a coach carrying German high-school students collided with a delivery van in the eastern Netherlands, Dutch police have said.

Eight people including the van driver were seriously hurt, while the remainder suffered minor injuries, the police department of the Gelderland region said. All were taken to hospital, it added.

The cause of the accident, near Wezep, to the east of Amsterdam, is under investigation. It is unclear how many of the wounded were students.

More than 50 students and four teachers were on the coach travelling to Paris from a school in the northern German town of Schönberg, according to a notice on its website.

The students belonged to two grade 12 classes - typically for those aged 17 to 18 years old - it added.

The school said there had been no reports of life-threatening injuries and that all of those involved were receiving comprehensive medical care.

Police said they received a report of a serious accident on the A28 near Wezep at around time 04:20 local time (02:20 GMT) on Monday.

The coach collided with a delivery van, crashed through the guardrail, and overturned onto its side, according to Dutch and German media, citing local police.

The A28 highway remains closed in both directions following the accident.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s MBS visits Macron in France: What to expect
articles.summary: Saudi crown prince and French president are set to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, (MBS), is on the second day of his two-day state visit to France, where he’s meeting President Emmanuel Macron.

In this explainer, we outline what they are expected to discuss and examine how their latest meetings build on an already evolving relationship.

MBS’s visit to Paris began on Sunday evening alongside President Macron at the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup. It was the first time the Esports tournament, which includes competitions ranging from video games to chess, had been held outside Saudi Arabia.

On Monday, Macron and Bin Salman are expected to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy.

French media reported that a deal to build a Dragon Ball-themed amusement park, backed by a Saudi investment fund and inspired by the iconic Japanese manga series, could be signed.

Valerie Pecresse, President of the Regional Council of Île-de-France in Greater Paris, told French broadcaster TF1 that the regional government had been working on the project for 18 months.

“There is a very important meeting at the Elysee today that may result in the signing of this agreement. We are waiting for the signature,” she said, describing the project as “on the scale of Disneyland”.

Bin Salman and Macron are also holding bilateral discussions on regional security and their economic ties.

That is expected to include discussions about energy routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz , such as new pipelines, capacity upgrades and alternative port networks.

France is a major buyer of Saudi oil and mineral products.

Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on February 28, shipping has been severely disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz – the vital waterway on which oil exporters in the Gulf are heavily reliant and where 20 percent of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies are shipped from during peacetime. The disruption sent oil prices soaring.

Before the war, a barrel of Brent crude – the global benchmark – cost about $66. Over the course of the conflict, prices have climbed above $100 – hitting a high of $119 early on in the war.

On Monday, Brent was trading around $93 a barrel.

Bin Salman and Macron are also expected to discuss the war in Iran, the bloodshed in Palestine, as well as developments in Syria and Lebanon, where Israel occupies around one-fifth of its territory.

Other expected topics on Monday’s agenda include global events that Saudi Arabia is set to host in the coming years, including Expo 2030, focusing on sustainability and urban innovation, and the 2034 football World Cup.

How much trade does Saudi Arabia do with France?

The two countries have a fairly equal trading balance.

In 2024, France exported $4.5bn worth of goods to Saudi Arabia and imported $4.6bn worth, according to data from the Observatory of Economic Complexity (OEC), an online platform that compiles and visualises international trade statistics.

Refined petroleum accounted for 72 percent of Saudi Arabia’s exports to France in 2024. Besides refined petroleum, Saudi Arabia exported crude petroleum and other mineral products to France. It also exported small amounts of machinery, chemicals and cars.

France’s exports to Saudi Arabia in 2024 were more diverse, including airliners, helicopters, gas turbines, pharmaceutical products and perfume, among other products.

What have relations between Saudi Arabia and France been like?

Sunday’s visit marked the third time MBS has visited France after trips in 2022 and 2023.

In December 2024, Macron visited Riyadh, where the two countries founded the Saudi-French Strategic Partnership Council, which formalised and upgraded political and economic ties between Saudi Arabia and France.

The current visit is also MBS’s first international trip since the August 7 signing of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, known as the Mecca pact – the mutual defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan.

Signed by the prince, Turkiye’s President, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistan’s Prime Minister, Shehbaz Sharif, the agreement commits all three states to treat an armed attack on any one of them as an attack on all three.

Analysts say the pact shows that Saudi Arabia is taking steps to diversify its security partnerships beyond Washington.

articles.title: Sonya Massey's killer Sean Grayson dies in US prison
articles.summary: The former police officer, whose crime reignited the debate about US police brutality, was undergoing treatment for cancer.
articles.body:
Sean Grayson, the white US police officer convicted of murdering a black woman, Sonya Massey, during an incident at her home in 2024, has died in prison at age 32.

Grayson shot dead Massey, 36, during an exchange that took place after she reported a suspected intruder at her residence in Illinois. The killing reignited the debate about police brutality in the US.

Grayson said he fired because he thought Massey was about to throw a pot of boiling water on him. He was last year found guilty of second-degree murder.

The former police officer was undergoing treatment for colon cancer. His lawyer Daniel Fultz confirmed to the BBC that Grayson had died on Sunday, but did not disclose the cause.

The Illinois Department of Corrections said it could only confirm that Grayson had died at a facility outside the state, and likewise did not provide a cause.

Lawyers for Massey's family said: "Grayson's death in custody from cancer does not bring Sonya back."

"We wish his family prayers of peace, as we do for all who grieve a loved one. Sonya's family knows that pain all too well and will grieve her loss the rest of their days," the lawyers said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

Protests took place across the US in the aftermath of Massey's death, and then-President Joe Biden declared that the late woman "should be alive today".

Ex-officer guilty of murder of Sonya Massey after she reported suspected intruder Published 29 October 2025

Ex-officer guilty of murder of Sonya Massey after she reported suspected intruder

The incident took place in the early hours over Independence Day weekend in July 2024. Massey called police to her home in Springfield, 200 miles (320km) south of Chicago, to report that she believed someone had broken in to her property.

Police bodycam footage of the incident showed the chaotic sequence of events.

The shooting happened after an exchange of words about a pot on Massey's stove. Massey and Grayson appeared to laugh over her pot of "steaming hot water", before Massey twice said: "I rebuke you in the name of Jesus."

"You better [expletive] not or I swear to God I'll [expletive] shoot you in your [expletive] face," Grayson said. He then drew his pistol as he shouted for her to drop the pot.

"OK, I'm sorry," Massey was heard saying before she ducked. Grayson fired three shots, striking her in the face.

Grayson, who was subsequently sacked from his job, was charged with first-degree murder, but the jury was allowed to convict him of the lesser charge of second-degree murder.

He was sentenced to 20 years in prison. In recent months, he applied for release on medical grounds, but was unsuccessful. He had been diagnosed with cancer in 2023.

articles.title: Rumours swirled after a Vietnamese teen was run over - then came a stunning admission
articles.summary: Confirmation of the circumstances around Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's death have only spurred more questions.
articles.body:
Until recently, there would have been little to distinguish Vietnam's so-called Justice Tree from the hundreds of others lining the streets of Hanoi. Then the bouquets started piling up.

It was here that former politician Nguyen Sy Cuong was driving his BMW in May last year when he veered into the opposite lane and smashed into a motorbike carrying a father and his teenage daughter.

The father, Do Viet Hung, suffered a broken leg but survived. The daughter, 18-year-old Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy, died in hospital 10 days after the collision, which severed her right leg.

Fifteen months later, her death and the silence surrounding it has become a lightning rod for discontent among Vietnam's youth.

In early August, a legion of anonymous social media users started publishing millions of posts with the hashtags #NguyenSyCuong and #BMW across Facebook, Instagram, Threads and X. The users identified themselves as Gen Z – and they demanded accountability.

Initial discussions circled around whether the former politician was in fact the one who had caused the accident, and why authorities had only released sparse information.

Some pointed to reports that the driver of the BMW had the initials NSC and was born in 1961, leading to speculation that he was a former member of parliament. Others claimed the incident had been swept under the rug due to the influence of powerful figures.

Many reported that their posts had been deleted by social media platforms at the request of the Vietnamese government – providing screenshots of notifications as evidence. These claims could not be independently verified.

Expressions of outrage and calls for a proper investigation grew in number, volume and force.

Meanwhile, masked flower bearers started to appear, gravitating towards the scene of the incident and laying vibrant bouquets at the base of what has now been dubbed the Justice Tree. Police quickly arrived to get rid of the flowers, prompting mourners to create a virtual equivalent of the tree online - where hundreds of thousands of people have since sent tributes and paid respects.

Pressurised by more than a year's worth of growing suspicion and a rush of online attention, the issue had become too big to ignore.

Then, last Monday, the government made an extraordinary admission.

State broadcaster Vietnam Television (VTV) televised an official statement from authorities, confirming what had happened on the day of the incident. Former National Assembly deputy Nguyen Sy Cuong was indeed driving his car down Nguyen Huy Tu Street on 30 May, 2025, when his vehicle suddenly swerved across the road and into an oncoming motorcycle.

VTV cited police and prosecution sources who said that because Nguyen Sy Cuong "sincerely confessed and actively and fully remedied the consequences of his actions", Do Ngoc Phuong Thuy's family had submitted a petition to exempt him from prosecution. The report did not specify what form this remedy took, but Nguyen Sy Cuong was cleared of all criminal liability.

While such a decision is lawful under Vietnam's legislation, lawyers have questioned whether the criminal proceedings were conducted in accordance with due process – or conducted at all. Social media users were quick to highlight his political connections and call for a more thorough investigation.

Such online pressure had yielded results in the past.

In March this year, a 66-year-old man driving under the influence of alcohol in Hanoi collided with seven other cars and three motorcycles in a chain-reaction crash that killed one woman and seriously injured two others.

In the wake of that incident, it emerged that the driver, Nguyen Van Sau, was a retired police colonel who had previously served as deputy director of a department under the Ministry of Public Security. Fearing that the driver was not being held culpable, the victim's family appealed for help. Social media users in turn amplified the issue, and after three months Nguyen Van Sau was charged with "violating regulations on participation in road traffic".

Who is To Lam, the ex-cop who wants to revamp Vietnam's success story?

British teen dies in reported Vietnam motorbike fall

Jailed Vietnamese tycoon's Birkin bags sell for more than $550K

Many now feel that a similar groundswell may be the only way to deliver justice for the teenager who died last year. But their efforts have been met with friction.

Do Viet Hung, the teenager's father, appeared in VTV's broadcast to thank internet users for their sympathy, but said the family was satisfied with the investigation's findings, and asked people to leave them alone. Notably, he also warned people "not to be drawn into the influence of reactionary elements".

Also appearing in the broadcast was a senior police official, who suggested that people were leveraging the incident to stoke dissent.

The Ministry of Public Security had "uncovered highly dangerous plots and intentions by hostile forces, reactionaries and bad actors to incite unrest and cause disorder", the official said.

"The ministry advises the public, especially young people, to remain fully alert and highly vigilant."

Similar rebukes have also started emerging on social media, with some claiming that conspiratorial forces were manipulating young people in Vietnam to stoke political discontent, manipulate public opinion online and rally people in real life ahead of the country's national holiday on 2 September.

Others have accused Gen Z Vietnamese of plotting a "colour revolution" – a term used to refer to mostly nonviolent protest movements that use specific colours or flowers as their symbol.

This is a familiar line of critique from Vietnamese authorities, who have previously labelled people's grievances or resentments as being untrue, unreasonable, or stemming from information fabricated by some "anti-government" or "reactionary" organisation.

Many in this case have said such accusations are baseless, insisting they are simply seeking justice for the victim of a fatal traffic accident. But the growing outrage has inevitably become a flashpoint amid broader, simmering grievances felt by Vietnam's youth.

Despite the Vietnamese government's tightening control over people's online freedom of expression – through measures ranging from intimidation and fines to criminal prosecution – public opinion in some corners has started to swerve against the Communist Party line.

On platforms such as Threads and Reddit, where anonymity is more normalised, many young people have expressed discontent towards various social issues: from the expansion of police power and land reclamation projects to exam cheating scandals and stricter regulation of online communication.

Such grievances echo those condemned by other Gen Z-led movements across the broader Asia region.

In countries like Bangladesh, India and Nepal, youth-led anti-government uprisings have over the past 12 months rallied immense support against the various pressure points of corruption, nepotism, economic inequality and democratic backsliding. Unofficially dubbed "the Asian Spring", the expanding influence of these movements has spread from Iran, Mongolia and the Maldives to the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

But protests in Vietnam have rarely, if ever, reached such fierce extremes. Vietnamese authorities have historically proven effective at detecting and stifling dissent before it boils over into action. Virtual places of mourning, anonymous social media posts, and online protests seem to be the most strident action many civilians here can afford to take.

Many are simply seeking justice for a teenager who was killed in a tragic accident, and accountability for a former lawmaker who appears to have been granted special clemency.

Yet even the mere suggestion that this incident could foment an uprising has provoked alarm – along with harsh reminders of the longstanding status quo in Vietnam's one-party state.

"Are these Gen Z kids planning a colour revolution using this accident?" reads one widely shared post. "Are they trying to emulate Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, and then create an Asian Spring? Remember, this is Vietnam! This is not Nepal, India, or Bangladesh!"

articles.title: In 1999, an American teacher donated $5,000 to a Chinese woman fighting desertification; with his support, she planted a 50,000-tree forest, and 27 years later, they reunited in tears
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 1999, American teacher Ronald Sakolsky was teaching English in Luoyang, China, when a television report about Yin Yuzhen, a woman battling desertif.
articles.body: In 1999, American teacher Ronald Sakolsky was teaching English in Luoyang, China, when a television report about Yin Yuzhen, a woman battling desertification in Inner Mongolia's Mu Us Sandy Land, moved him deeply. He decided to help and spent about two months raising $5,000 through a US-based charity to support Yin's tree-planting work. The money helped her buy saplings as she and her family continued their efforts to hold back the desert. Over the years, the trees grew into a forest of more than 50,000 trees. Sakolsky and Yin first met in person in 2000 but eventually lost touch for more than two decades. In 2026, Yin searched for her old American friend online. Their efforts to reconnect succeeded, and on August 23, 2026, the two finally met again at an airport in Ordos, Inner Mongolia, where they embraced and cried.How an American teacher's $5,000 helped plant a 50,000-tree forestSakolsky was working as an English teacher in Luoyang under a China-US teacher exchange programme when he saw a television report about Yin's struggle against the advancing desert sands. Yin and her husband had been planting trees in the Mu Us Sandy Land, an area where desertification had made farming and daily life extremely difficult. Moved by her determination, Sakolsky decided that he wanted to contribute to the effort. He spent around two months contacting organisations in the US before a Boston-based charity agreed to provide $5,000. The money was sent to support Yin's afforestation work, helping her purchase saplings for planting in the sandy landscape. Sakolsky did not expect the contribution to make him famous or bring him any financial return. He simply wanted to support someone trying to restore degraded land.Yin turned the donation into a long-term fight against desertificationYin used the money for tree planting and continued the work for decades. Reports say the trees associated with Sakolsky's contribution eventually grew into a forest of more than 50,000 trees. It is important, however, to distinguish this forest from Yin's much larger restoration effort. She had begun planting trees years before receiving Sakolsky's support and continued planting for decades afterwards. Xinhua reports that Yin planted her first sapling in 1986 and has spent roughly four decades working to combat desertification in the region. Her broader efforts have helped green more than 70,000 mu of sandy land, equivalent to roughly 4,667 hectares.The transformation was gradual. Trees in sandy landscapes require years of planting, watering and protection before they can become established. Yin and her family continued caring for the trees long after the original donation had been spent. What began as an act of support from an American teacher therefore became part of a much longer local effort to stabilise the land and create vegetation where desert conditions had prevailed.The American teacher and Chinese woman met in 2000Sakolsky eventually travelled to Inner Mongolia and met Yin in person in 2000. During the visit, he saw the landscape where she was planting trees and learned more about the difficulties involved in restoring the sandy land. The meeting gave him a direct connection to the work he had supported from thousands of kilometres away. Photographs from the period later became an important part of the story when the two were reunited decades later.After their meeting, however, the two gradually lost contact. Sakolsky eventually returned to the US, while Yin remained in Inner Mongolia and continued her environmental work. More than two decades passed without the pair seeing each other. Their connection survived through memories of their first meeting and the forest that had grown from the broader tree-planting effort.Yin searched for her old friend after more than two decadesIn May 2026, Yin posted a video online looking for Sakolsky. She wanted to reconnect with the American teacher who had supported her tree-planting work and hoped he could return to China to see the forest for himself. Her appeal spread online and eventually helped locate Sakolsky. The two reconnected through a video call, giving them their first direct conversation in many years. Yin reportedly told him that she wanted him to come back and see the trees that had grown since their first meeting.The reunion also allowed Sakolsky to see how dramatically the landscape had changed. The man who had once seen Yin's story on television could now see that the small contribution he had made had become part of a much larger environmental legacy. He subsequently travelled back to China, with Inner Mongolia among the destinations on his journey.They reunited in tears after 27 yearsOn August 23, 2026, Sakolsky arrived at Ordos Ejin Horo International Airport in Inner Mongolia, where Yin and members of her family were waiting for him. When the two saw each other again, they embraced and became emotional. Reports described both of them crying during the reunion. Sakolsky, now 69, described the moment as a dream come true.The reunion came roughly 27 years after Sakolsky first became involved in Yin's story in 1999, although their first face-to-face meeting occurred in 2000. During his visit, Sakolsky also planned to return to the area where he had first seen Yin's tree-planting work and plant trees with her. The story that began with a $5,000 contribution had come full circle.Sakolsky provided financial support at a crucial moment, while Yin and her family spent decades planting, watering and protecting trees. The resulting forest became a lasting symbol of that connection and ultimately helped bring two people who had lost touch for decades back together.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 76 percent in Canada say ending US trade negotiations was right call: Survey
articles.summary: More than three-quarters of Canadians believe their country ending trade negotiations with the U.S. was the right call, according to a new poll. In the Angus Reid Institute poll, 76 percent of respondents said their country was in the right “by refusing the terms being offered and ending negotiations without a trade agreement,” while 13…
articles.body:
More than three-quarters of Canadians believe their country ending trade negotiations with the U.S. was the right call, according to a new poll .

In the Angus Reid Institute poll , 76 percent of respondents said their country was in the right “by refusing the terms being offered and ending negotiations without a trade agreement,” while 13 percent said the opposite. Eleven percent were unsure about Canada’s decision.

On Friday evening, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney removed his country’s negotiators from trade discussions with the U.S., shortly before a new round of tariffs from the Trump administration went into effect.

The Canadian prime minister then said Saturday his country would implement retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. starting Sept. 8, responding to the Trump administration’s new 50 percent duties. The American tariffs impose a 50 percent levy on more than $20 billion’s worth of goods from the U.S.’s northern neighbor, impacting products like wine and cement.

During a press conference, Carney said Ottawa would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

President Trump on Sunday claimed Canada desires the “benefits of being a state, without being one” in a Truth Social post, referencing his previous talk of acquiring the country as the U.S.’s 51st state.

In the Angus Reid Institute poll, 6 percent said they were “very confident” in the idea “that Canada and the United States will eventually be able to reach a new trade agreement,” while 33 percent were “confident,” 48 percent were “not confident” and 14 percent were unsure about their confidence level.

The Angus Reid Institute poll took place from Aug. 22-23, featuring 1,468 Canadian adults and a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

articles.title: Two National Trust visitor centres and cafes to shut
articles.summary: The charity says the cafes and visitor centres at Robin Hood's Bay and Ravenscar are no longer viable.
articles.body:
Two National Trust visitor centres and cafes on the North Yorkshire coast will close next month, the charity has confirmed.

Old Coastguard Station in Robin Hood's Bay and a second site in Ravenscar are considered "no longer viable in the long term" by the charity, despite efforts to improve their performance.

According to the National Trust, both sites will cease trading and close to customers on 6 September.

The decision has resulted in a "number of roles" being made redundant, which followed a period of consultation with staff.

A National Trust spokesperson said: "Like many hospitality businesses, we have faced significant challenges in recent years.

"Despite efforts to improve performance, these cafés are no longer viable in the long term.

"As a charity, we have a responsibility to use our resources effectively so we can continue to deliver our conservation work."

Andy Hill, from Cloughton, often visits the Ravenscar visitor centre with his wife and said he was "disappointed" by the news of its closure.

"We've seen it packed out by families, older people who want a coffee and a look at the view, it's really nice," the 75-year-old said.

"A lot of people stop there because it's halfway between Scarborough and Whitby.

"It's just a big shock. There will be nobody to give advice on how to get down the coast safely or how to see a seal colony."

The National Trust spokesperson added: "We know this news will be disappointing for staff, local communities and visitors.

"We remain committed to helping people enjoy the Yorkshire coast and will work with colleagues, communities and stakeholders to explore future opportunities for these buildings and how they can best support our ambitions for the North Yorkshire coast."

They thanked staff for their dedication and professionalism at the venues over many years.

articles.title: Iran threatens 45 tankers with fines, confiscation in Hormuz escalation
articles.summary: By Nidhi Verma and Florence Tan Aug 24 (Reuters) - Iran said it had blacklisted 45 tankers that had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz, and w...
articles.body:
Aug 24 (Reuters) - Iran said it had blacklisted 45 tankers that had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz, and would take action against any vessels ‌transferring loads with them, escalating its threats over the key waterway six months into the war.

The named ‌vessels could be fined, detained and have their cargoes confiscated, according to an X post late on Sunday from the Persian Gulf Strait ​Authority, a new body set up by Iran to manage the strait.

The warning was issued within days of the U.S. threatening Iran with "the toughest sanctions in history", and Iran saying its response to any new U.S. threats would be "devastating".

The restricted list includes very large crude carriers, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, and clean product vessels, among others.

Some of ‌the named ships are owned by the ⁠United Arab Emirates' ADNOC Logistics and Shipping (ADNOC L&S), ADNOC's subsidiary Navig8 Tankers, and Saudi Arabia's national shipping carrier Bahri.

Any vessels involved in ship-to-ship transfers with the named vessels could be ⁠added to the blacklist, the Iranian X post added.

The post did not spell out what it meant by Iran's rules, but Tehran has in the past said ship-owners should get its clearance to transit the strait and said ships should pay for ​security and ​other services.

The U.S. has also imposed a naval blockade against ​Iran-related shipping.

The Gulf supplied about 20% of the ‌world's daily crude oil and liquefied natural gas before the Iran conflict disrupted tanker traffic.

U.S.-coordinated efforts to shuttle tankers quietly through the Strait of Hormuz to fill supertankers waiting just outside it are helping restore some of those export volumes.

U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said on X on Friday that the "7-day average of oil leaving the Strait is over 8 million barrels a day. Make no mistake, thanks to the U.S. Navy, oil is flowing through the ‌Strait of Hormuz."

Ships owned by Klaveness Ship Management, Stolt Tankers and ​South Korea's Sinokor were also included on the blacklist.

ADNOC declined to comment, ​while other shipping firms did not immediately respond ​to Reuters' requests for comment.

The Persian Gulf Strait Authority has said cargo owners should refer ‌to an updated list of vessels deemed non-compliant ​for voyages relating to the Gulf.

Ships ​seeking the removal of their names from the non-compliant vessels' list must submit a request with relevant explanations to Iran's maritime authorities, the post said.

articles.title: Algeria’s schools put Shakespeare before Molière in break from France
articles.summary: Algerian primary schools will begin teaching English before French for the first time, signalling a drift from France.
articles.body:
Ahmed Krim spent 30 years teaching English in Algeria’s middle schools. Now retired, the 60-year-old watched the language he loved remain firmly behind French as the country’s second language.

English was less valued than French, which might have been the language of Algeria’s coloniser, but continues to be present in every dialogue, six decades after independence.

On July 25 , Algeria’s Education Minister, Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui, announced that English will become the sole foreign language taught in the third year of primary school in the new academic year for 2026-2027.

French would be pushed back to the fourth year, ending its domination of foreign language classes in Algerian schools.

From next month, eight-year-olds across Algeria will become the first to learn English before French.

“It is a very good decision. But it requires thinking, planning and resources,” Krim told Al Jazeera.

It is among the first steps in President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s linguistic overhaul for Algeria, which he first outlined in 2022 with English being introduced to primary schools.

Since then, medicine and science faculties have begun switching from French to English.

The French language has been erased from some utility bills and Air Algerie tickets. Road signs are beginning to feature English alongside Arabic, while government ministers’ websites will also have English as an option.

The shift from French to English as Algeria’s secondary language is both sweeping and structural.

It comes amid the most serious diplomatic crisis between the two countries since Algeria’s independence from France in 1962.

In July 2024, French President Emmanuel Macron publicly backed Morocco’s sovereignty claim over Western Sahara.

Algeria, which supports the Sahrawi Polisario Front and hosts over 170,000 Sahrawi refugees, viewed that as highly provocative.

That, and other issues, saw Algeria expel French diplomats , and vice versa.

Algeria’s replacement of French as the country’s second language accelerated after the diplomatic crisis grew.

A rethink of the whole education system in Algeria may be needed.

“First and foremost, specialised training centres must be restored and candidates must not be forced into the teaching profession without wanting it – we need people who genuinely want to do this work,” Krim said.

He refers to dedicated institutes established after independence, where primary and middle school teachers, like himself, trained via a model that combined classroom instruction with direct school placements to meet the gap in Arabic instructors.

The centres operated until the late 1990s, when an economic crunch replaced them with the fewer and more selective Ecoles Normales Superieures.

Most teachers today are university graduates, but lack the practical, classroom-first grounding that the older model provided.

Krim said that school curricula must be designed and entrusted to “a qualified body that includes both linguistic and pedagogical expertise, free from all ideology”.

But journalist and analyst Noureddine Bessadi said the ideological dimension matters in Algeria, which overthrew colonialism following a bloody and bitter struggle against the French.

“Since independence in 1962, every shift in language policy has been fought as much on political as pedagogical grounds,” Bessadi told Al Jazeera.

After independence, Algeria’s Arabisation drive, when French was displaced from government and education, was “part of state building and enforcing Algeria’s identity, centring Arabic and Islam”, Bessadi added.

Tamazight, a non-Semitic language spoken by around a quarter of Algeria’s population, was marginalised until 1995, Bessadi said, shaped by an “ideological perception of unity that prioritised linguistic and cultural harmony”.

Critics argue that the transition from French to English is happening faster than the system can keep up with. For one, it is believed that there are not enough qualified English teachers to make the language reforms work.

But one source familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that there are enough teachers to roll out this programme in primary schools and that any shortage could be filled through contractors.

In February, Algeria’s education ministry reportedly recruited about 15,000 English language teachers for primary schools.

Rafik Laceb, a lecturer in English at Mouloud Mammeri University in Tizi Ouzou, is cautiously optimistic about the primary school reform. But he considers the parallel push to teach university subjects in English to be rushed and poorly executed.

“Frankly, and beyond any chauvinism, I believe this decision is positive… I believe there is, today, sufficient supervision and evaluation work from the first experience,” Laceb said, in reference to the previous introduction of English in later primary school years.

The university experiment that began in 2023-2024 produced insufficient contact hours, a lack of genuine assessment of students’ English levels and no tracking of their progress.

Around 50 percent of teaching at Tizi Ouzou University’s English department is by younger contract staff, which brings other challenges.

“A young contract teacher must first master the basic principles of medicine before attempting to teach medical terminology in English,” he said.

Currently, children only begin learning a foreign language in the third year of state primary schools, whereas multiple languages are taught at private schools from kindergarten.

Djamel Merah, whose daughter attended private schools before transferring to public secondary school, studied Arabic, French and English simultaneously from kindergarten level.

Merah welcomes the government’s language reforms at state primary schools, which will provide more children with the opportunity to learn English.

“It addresses a question about the gap in opportunities between children who get multilingual education from the start and those in public schools who don’t get the same chance,” he said.

There also appears to be a more organic response among the public that precedes the government’s promotion of the English language.

Krimo Taleb, a bookseller at the Libre Pensee bookshop in Tizi Ouzou, has seen a growth in English-language book sales, particularly among female readers.

“In my opinion, it has nothing to do with government decisions. The majority of young readers today speak three languages fluently,” he said.

His own daughter, a middle school student, reads fluently in Arabic, English and French.

Colleen Hoover, Ana Huang and J. K. Rowling are some of the best-selling authors at his shop.

“Previously, our bookshops provided for English literature students the works of Shakespeare,” Taleb says. “Today, there is a diverse range of English-language titles aimed at the general public.”

However, French remains Algeria’s most influential foreign language. According to the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), Algeria has approximately 15 million French speakers, nearly a third of its population.

There is not a single newspaper published in English and written English by Algerians remains in its infancy.

But there are signs that former colonies are turning their backs on France’s linguistic legacy, particularly in Africa, where Paris’s military and political presence made a resurgence in recent decades .

In March 2025, Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso withdrew from the OIF, accusing it of being a political instrument of Paris.

“Mali made its national languages official in 2023, demoting French to a working language. Burkina Faso followed the same year and Niger in 2025,” Bessadi added. “Even Senegal, which has not removed French as an official language, has begun encouraging local languages at its expense.”

For Krim, Algeria’s linguistic ambitions are not far-fetched, but for it to work, the country needs the “necessary resources… and transparency”.

The municipality replaced French-language signage in March last year, a quiet but pointed act of linguistic reclamation in a town once so thoroughly colonised it was nicknamed 'Little Paris' by French settlers who arrived in 1830 [File: Madjid Serrah/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: In 1998, Costa Rica spread 12,000 tonnes of orange waste over degraded pasture; 16 years later, tree diversity had tripled and forest biomass was 176% higher
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In the late 1990s, an unusual conservation experiment began in Costa Rica when ecologists proposed using orange peels and pulp to help restore a badly.
articles.body: In the late 1990s, an unusual conservation experiment began in Costa Rica when ecologists proposed using orange peels and pulp to help restore a badly degraded piece of land inside a national park.For this, orange juice company Del Oro and ecologists Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs, worked with the Area de Conservacion Guanacaste (ACG), or Guanacaste Conservation Area. According to Princeton University, the company had recently started production near the northern border of the conservation area and was looking for a way to deal with its orange waste.Janzen and Hallwachs proposed a deal wherein Del Oro would donate some of its forested land to the ACG. In return, the company could take its orange peel waste to a degraded pasture inside the park, where it could break down naturally.After the agreement was signed, around 1,000 truckloads of orange peels and pulp, totalling about 12,000 metric tonnes, were spread across the degraded land.Over the next several years, the area changed dramatically. A place that had once been covered by exposed rock and dead grass became a dense forest filled with trees, vines and other vegetation.A forest emergesThe site was largely forgotten after the orange waste was deposited. A rival orange juice company, TicoFruit, later sued Del Oro, arguing that the company had defiled a national park. The case reached Costa Ricaâs Supreme Court, which ruled in favour of TicoFruit.The legal dispute meant that the site received little attention for about 15 years. That changed in 2013, when Princeton University researcher Timothy Treuer was discussing possible research projects with Janzen.Janzen mentioned the orange-peel site to Treuer and said that although taxonomists had visited the area, it had not received a thorough evaluation. Treuer decided to visit it during another research trip to Costa Rica.When he arrived, the site looked completely different from what he expected. The vegetation had grown so densely that Treuer could not initially see the large sign marking the experiment.âIt was so completely overgrown with trees and vines that I couldnât even see the 7-foot-long sign with bright yellow lettering marking the site that was only a few feet from the road,â Treuer said, as quoted by Princeton.The contrast became even clearer when Treuer compared the orange-peel site with the nearby untreated pasture. The treated area had become a thick forest, while the neighbouring land remained much more open.âIt was just hard to believe that the only difference between the two areas was a bunch of orange peels. They look like completely different ecosystems,â Treuer explained.Researchers assess forestTreuer worked with Jonathan Choi, then a Princeton student studying ecology and evolutionary biology. The researchers compared the area treated with orange waste with a nearby untreated pasture. They also collected and analysed soil samples from both sites to determine whether the orange waste had changed the soil over time.They also measured vegetation in both areas. The team established 100-metre-long lines, known as transects, through the forest. Trees growing within three metres of these lines were measured and identified. The same approach was used in the untreated pasture across the road.The differences were substantial. The soil in the orange-waste area was richer in nutrients. The area also had greater tree biomass, more tree species and a more closed forest canopy.The study found a 176% increase in aboveground biomass within the three-hectare area that was examined. Aboveground biomass refers to the wood and other plant material growing above the soil, including the trees.The researchers also found a major difference in tree diversity. While the surrounding areas were dominated by one type of tree, the former orange-waste site had about two dozen species of vegetation.Wildlife returned to restored areaThe changes were not limited to plants. Researchers also found signs of a more developed ecosystem at the site. Among the discoveries was a tayra, a dog-sized mammal related to weasels, Diario AS reported. The researchers also found a huge fig tree that had grown in the area.Jonathan Choi described the site as even more impressive in person than he had expected. âWhile I would walk over exposed rock and dead grass in the nearby fields, Iâd have to climb through undergrowth and cut paths through walls of vines in the orange peel site itself.âThe size of the fig tree was another indication of how much the area had changed. Choi said the tree was about three feet in diameter and described it as massive. âYou could have had 20 people climbing in that tree at once and it would have supported the weight no problem. That thing was massive,â he said.The researchers published their findings in the journal Restoration Ecology in a paper titled âLow-Cost Agricultural Waste Accelerates Tropical Forest Regenerationâ.Timothy Treuer said the experiment was unusual because it showed that forest restoration and waste management could potentially work together. âThis is one of the only instances Iâve ever heard of where you can have cost-negative carbon sequestration,â Treuer said. âItâs not just a win-win between the company and the local park; itâs a win for everyone.âThe researchers, however, did not suggest that companies should simply take their waste and dump it in natural areas. Treuer specifically warned against such an approach. âWe donât want companies to go out there willy-nilly just dumping their waste all over the place,â Treuer said. âBut if itâs scientifically driven and restorationists are involved in addition to companies, this is something I think has really high potential.âCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nigeria drug arrests: '101-year-old great-grandmother' detained for selling cannabis
articles.summary: Esther Ogunmabo is accused of selling "retail sachets" of a strain of cannabis known as skunk.
articles.body:
An elderly woman, who the authorities say is 101, has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly selling cannabis, in a case that has drawn widespread attention.

Esther Ogunmabo, described as a great-grandmother, was apprehended on Saturday in Ogun state, in the south-west of the country, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) announced.

Femi Babafemi, the agency's media director, said the centenarian was found with "retail sachets of skunk, a strain of cannabis weighing 90 grams, which she claims she sells to locals".

The NDLEA said the suspect told investigators that she turned to the illicit drug trade after her provisions shop was destroyed by fire. She has been released on bail.

According to the Ndlea, one of her daughters, who lives in Lagos, allegedly arranged for the supply of the substance to her every four days. Ogunmabo is accused of then selling it on in smaller quantities to customers in her community.

Ndlea chief executive Mohamed Marwa directed that the suspect be granted bail and given counselling because of her advanced age.

Ogunmabo’s bail status means she could still be charged for criminal activity.

Ogunmabo’s arrest came as the Ndlea also reported significant drug seizures along Nigeria's maritime routes.

In Akwa Ibom state, operatives acting on credible intelligence intercepted a wooden boat on the high seas last Friday, which was heading to Cameroon, and arrested three people on board.

More than 42kg of narcotics were recovered from the suspects.

In what the agency described as a milestone, the Ndlea also recorded its first-ever seizure of illicit drugs shipped from Thailand.

articles.title: Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza
articles.summary: Hamas says the kites found in Israeli border communities in recent days were launched by children in Gaza.
articles.body:
Israel has warned Hamas that it will increase strikes on Gaza following concern over launches of kites, drones and balloons from the territory.

Several kites were found in an Israeli community near the border with Gaza over the weekend, local media reported.

"Forceful actions will be taken to put an end to this phenomenon," Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Monday.

Before the war, kites and balloons carrying incendiary devices were launched into Israel, causing fires that burned forest and farmland.

Hamas has denied responsibility for the new kites - which were not carrying explosives - and said they belonged to "children searching for their innocent childhood amid the rubble".

The group also accused Israel of using the kites as a "pretext" for continued air strikes in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreed last October.

Four kites were found in Kibbutz Nahal Oz, which is about 800m (2,620ft) from the Gaza border, on Friday and Saturday. Several more were found elsewhere in southern Israel last week, according to local media.

The Israeli reports cited military sources as saying they believed Hamas was behind the kites and that they might have been intended to test Israel's response.

No suspicious materials were attached to the kites and they did not pose a threat, the military said.

But Katz warned there would be "zero tolerance" and said: "A balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone, with or without explosives."

Residents of Nahal Oz said in a statement that they feared the return of incendiary kites and balloons, adding: "We will not accept a policy of containment when it comes to our security."

Hamas warned of "the danger of the allegations and threats" from Israel and said the kites were "basically children's toys from displacement camps".

"These threats are based on fabricated pretexts and are an attempt to justify the continuation of the aggression and violations against our people," a spokesman for the group added.

On Sunday, Palestinian health officials said two people were killed and seven others injured in two Israeli strikes in Nuseirat refugee camp and the town of al-Zawayda, both in central Gaza.

A four-year-old boy called Mohammed Taha was killed when a building in al-Zawayda, just north of Maghazi refugee camp, was bombed, according to local media.

The Israeli military said it killed the commander of a Hamas weapons manufacturing site in the Maghazi area, whom it identified as Ismail Abu Ful, and that it had warned the residents to evacuate beforehand.

"There is no ceasefire, there is nothing," Abu Ahmed, a displaced man who had been sheltering nearby, told Reuters news agency. "We want solutions, we want to live in peace."

On Monday, Palestinian media reported that a man called Mohammed Abu Asad was killed in an overnight Israeli strike on a tent in the central town of Deir al-Balah.

The Israeli military said Abu Asad was a member of the elite Nukhba forces of Hamas's military wing who had taken part in the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the cross-border assault, during which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

More than 74,420 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including 1,288 since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

articles.summary: South Asia News: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city, with investigators uncovering disturbing details abou.
articles.body: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city, with investigators uncovering disturbing details about the killings and an alleged attempt to destroy evidence.The victims were identified as retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, their 23-year-old daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi and their 12-year-old son Priyam Chakraborty. Their bodies were recovered from their home in the Daspara (Machhuapara) area at around 11.30pm on Saturday.According to Bangladeshâs The Daily Star, Pritilataâs younger sister Puja Chakraborty said the family noticed that the victimsâ faces had been burnt when the bodies were handed over to them.âWhen we received the bodies in the evening, we found that their faces had been burned. Earlier, police did not allow us to go near the bodies,â Puja said.Sumit Chowdhury, acting superintendent of police of CID Rangpur, told The Daily Star that investigators suspected a flammable substance had been used on the victimsâ faces.âThe killers appear to have poured a flammable substance on the victimsâ faces either before or after killing them. At this stage, we cannot say what substance was used. The investigating officer will collect samples and send them to the CID forensic department for examination. We will know more once the test results are available.âThe bodies were found in different parts of the house. The mother and daughter were found on the staircase, Ganapatiâs body was recovered from the roof, while Priyam was found under a bed. Police initially suspected that the family had been strangled, with the killings believed to have taken place between midnight on Thursday and early Friday.Investigators said suspects Mugdha and Siddhartha allegedly remained inside the house after the killings. According to Prothom Alo, they reportedly bathed there, ate dates and cucumbers from the refrigerator and used yaba before leaving on Friday during Jummah prayers, when the streets were relatively quiet.Police also found cupboards and drawers opened and belongings scattered, suggesting an attempt to make the killings appear to be a robbery. Evidence allegedly indicated an attempt to test a gold bangle using fire, while two phones belonging to the victims had been submerged in water mixed with detergent, apparently to destroy evidence.The suspects were detained based on these clues and allegedly confessed during questioning, police said. Gold jewellery believed to have been stolen was later recovered from an abandoned location they identified. Date pits found inside the house have also been sent for DNA testing, according to Prothom Alo.Puja said the family had not been heard from since Thursday and all four phones were switched off. Police later broke open the locked main gate and found the bodies.Police, CID and Detective Branch teams are jointly investigating the case, while preparations were under way to file a murder case.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Shelley Fabares, ‘Johnny Angel’ singer and actor on ‘The Donna Reed Show’ and ‘Coach,’ dies at 82
articles.summary: Fabares died Saturday in Los Angeles, her family said. No cause was given.
articles.body: Shelley Fabares, an actor who was a fixture on television for decades from her days as a young teenager on “The Donna Reed Show,” through “One Day at a Time” and “Coach,” has died. She was 82. She died Saturday in Los Angeles, her family said in a statement to The Associated Press. No cause was given. “To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter, and comfort,” her family wrote. “She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued, and cared for.” Fabares was born in Santa Monica, California, in 1944, and started acting as a young child. Her first television credit came at age 10 when she appeared on “The Loretta Young Show.” Many movies and television shows followed: She acted with Paul Newman, Frank Sinatra and Eva Marie Saint in a Producers Showcase production of “Our Town” and was in the Rosalind Russell movie “The Girl Rush” and the Rock Hudson drama “Never Say Goodbye.” Other early credits include “Annette,” “Captain Midnight” and the “Black Leather Jackets” episode of “The Twilight Zone.” Her biggest break came when she was cast as Mary Stone on “The Donna Reed Show,” where she was a regular from 1958 through 1963. During that time she also got a recording contract and had two Top 40 hits, including “Johnny Angel.” In the early 1960s, she also co-starred in three movies with Elvis Presley: “Girl Happy,” “Spinout” and “Clambake.” “I think the years on ‘The Donna Reed Show,’ the years from 14 to 19, were so incredibly important,” Fabares told the Los Angeles Times in 1993. “Donna Reed was simply an extraordinary woman, a woman of great strength, kindness, integrity and compassion. I am not trying to make her sound like a saint, but she had the most profound influence on me. I carry her with me today.” In the late 1970s, Fabares made an impression as Francine Webster on the CBS sitcom “One Day at a Time.” She also played James Caan’s wife in “Brian’s Song.” One of her biggest roles came when she was cast as Christine Armstrong in “Coach,” although the show took a minute to find its audience. “I did always feel from the very beginning if they could find the right spot for us, this was a show that would last,” she said in the 1993 Los Angeles Times interview. Fabares married twice, first to producer Lou Adler in 1964. She had been married to “M-A-S-H” actor Mike Farrell since 1984. She was also a devoted advocate for Alzheimer’s awareness, which affected her mother. In early 1999, a visit to the emergency room for an esophageal bleed revealed that she had progressive liver failure. After spending 22 months on a waiting list, she had liver transplant surgery in October 2000. In an interview with Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles three years after the transplant, she said she’d been “changed by the experience” and was eternally grateful to Farrell, who was with her “every step of the way.” Her family, in their statement, said that “we will remember Shelley for her kindness, loyalty, wit, courage, and beautiful spirit. We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives.”

articles.title: Royal Shakespeare Company backs plan for £600m theme park near Bicester
articles.summary: A company submitted a planning application for the attraction in the Oxfordshire countryside last year.
articles.body:
The Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) has backed plans to build a £600m history-based theme park in the Oxfordshire countryside.

French firm Puy du Fou submitted proposals to build the site, north of Bicester, to Cherwell District Council last year.

The RSC described the proposal as an "exciting opportunity to further enhance the UK's cultural and tourism offer".

Puy du Fou has said it aims to open the park in phases, beginning in 2029 and that it would employ about 2,000 people. Its plans have sparked concerns from some locals, who have expressed fears about the impact the site will have on things such as traffic and wildlife.

A new group has also been created to bring together representatives from Heyford Park and surrounding villages to discuss the impact of major schemes planned in the area, including the theme park.

The forum, approved by Oxfordshire County Council, wants to help prevent the area from "descending into traffic gridlock".

But Blenheim Palace , national tourism agency VisitBritain , performing arts and entertainment trade union Equity , and Experience Oxfordshire, are among those who have previously backed the theme park plan.

The Puy du Fou attraction would include four period villages and 13 live shows in which visitors could "immerse themselves in British history".

Developers estimate the attraction could welcome up to 1.4 million visitors a year once fully open.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

In a letter seen by the BBC, issued by the RSC's senior leadership team to the council, and confirmed by the organisation as authentic, it said: "We recognise the important role that major cultural and visitor attractions can play in strengthening the regional economy, increasing tourism, creating employment opportunities, and encouraging wider participation in arts, culture, and heritage.

"There is currently no equivalent attraction operating at this scale within the UK, and we can see the potential for the project to attract new visitors to the region, generate economic activity, and contribute to the continued growth of the visitor economy across the Midlands and surrounding areas."

The letter said the RSC was "particularly encouraged by the potential for collaboration across the cultural, tourism, hospitality, and education sectors".

"Major attractions often act as catalysts for wider partnerships, helping organisations work together to create richer visitor experiences and strengthen the overall appeal of a destination," it added.

The RSC concluded that it supported the "ambitions" of the project and the "potential benefits it could bring to the region, its communities, and the wider visitor economy".

Puy du Fou has had history-themed parks in Les Epesses in France since 1978 and in Toledo, Spain, since 2021.

articles.title: Washington Post ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after being terminated over Charlie Kirk posts
articles.summary: The Washington Post has been ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after being fired for Bluesky posts about Charlie Kirk's assassination.
articles.body: The Washington Post was ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after she was fired last year for social media posts she made after Charlie Kirk's assassination. Sarah Miller Espinosa, the arbitrator overseeing Attiah's legal challenge against The Post, said the paper "did not have good and sufficient cause" and that it "violated" her labor agreement, according to The New York Times, which first reported on Espinosa's ruling last Thursday. "The Washington Post failed to establish the grievant engaged in gross misconduct," Espinosa concluded. TEACHERS WHO CELEBRATED CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION NOW CASH IN WITH TAXPAYER-FUNDED SETTLEMENTS Attiah told The Times she is "relieved to finally have that record set straight," adding, "This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion writer, and this was wrongful termination." The columnist announced her legal victory, saying on X, "The Washington Post fired me last year for speaking the truth after Charlie Kirk's killing. I fought back. I'm happy to announce: I won my case against the Washington Post. They have been ordered to reinstate me immediately." "In general, if someone reveals themselves to be a ghoul then companies should be able to fire them," Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet told Fox News Digital.  A spokesperson for The Washington Post said the paper respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further. Attiah didn't immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Attiah sparked outrage for her posts about the slain conservative icon on the liberal social media platform Bluesky. TENNESSEE UNIVERSITY TO PAY PROFESSOR $1.9M AFTER CALLING CHARLIE KIRK A 'DISGUSTING PSYCHOPATH' GEORGIA TEACHER RECEIVES ALMOST $300K SETTLEMENT OVER CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION POST "Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a White man that espoused violence is… not the same as violence," Attiah wrote at the time. In a separate post, she wrote, "Part of what keeps America so violent is the insistence that people perform care, empty goodness and absolution for White men who espouse hatred and violence.’" Critics also slammed Attiah for misquoting Kirk in another post, attributing to him saying, "Black women do not have the brain processing power to be taken seriously. You have to go steal a White person's slot." On a July 2023 episode of "The Charlie Kirk Show," Kirk actually said, "If we would have said three weeks ago [...] that Joy Reid and Michelle Obama, and Sheila Jackson Lee, and Ketanji Brown Jackson were affirmative-action picks, we would have been called racist. But now they're comin' out and they're saying it for us! They're comin' out, and they're saying, 'I'm only here because of affirmative action.' Yeah, we know. You do not have the brain processing power to otherwise be taken really seriously. You had to go steal a White person's slot to go be taken somewhat seriously." Following the backlash, Attiah revealed she had been fired by The Post, saying in a termination letter her posts were "unacceptable" and "gross misconduct."
